title: After jacking up prices, Disney+ and Netflix consider offering free alternatives
gist: Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro confirmed the company is exploring a free ad-supported streaming product to reach price-sensitive customers and boost ad revenue, while Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said a free tier could work in some markets but risks cannibalizing paid subscriptions — both moves coming after years of repeated price hikes that have pushed 70% of surveyed US/Canada respondents toward ad-supported or free FAST services.

themes.theme: Disney's pivot toward a free streaming tier

insights.claim: Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro confirmed the company is 'exploring a free product' for streaming customers, describing it as a way to reach more 'price-sensitive' customers, which he called a 'strategic priority' for Disney, though he said there is 'nothing specific to announce today.'
insights.speaker: Josh D’Amaro (via Scharon Harding)
insights.so_what: A confirmed strategic priority (not yet a committed product) to launch a free tier is a forward-looking signal for Disney's streaming ad-revenue growth strategy and a potential new customer acquisition funnel, worth tracking for a formal announcement.
insights.quote: A free offering could help us drive top-of-funnel Disney+ subscriber growth.

insights.claim: D’Amaro said a free streaming service would generate more ad revenue, noting that Disney is 'fairly well-sold' on inventory unlike many AVOD competitors, meaning more ad inventory from a free tier would directly accelerate ad revenue growth.
insights.speaker: Josh D’Amaro (via Scharon Harding)
insights.so_what: Disney explicitly framing itself as inventory-constrained (not demand-constrained) on advertising is a specific supply-side signal that a free tier's primary value would be unlocking incremental ad revenue rather than just subscriber growth — relevant for modeling Disney's streaming ad business upside.
insights.quote: Unlike a lot of our AVOD [advertising video on demand] competitors, we’re fairly well-sold, meaning more inventory would actually help us accelerate our ad revenue growth.

insights.claim: A Business Insider report cited in the article claimed Disney was discussing making some Disney+ content accessible without a paywall, and that Adam Smith, Disney's chief product and technology officer, discussed free streaming content during an internal meeting for streaming employees, without sharing a timeline or scope.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding (citing Business Insider)
insights.so_what: Internal discussion reaching streaming-team employees (beyond just investor-call rhetoric) suggests the free-tier initiative has moved past pure speculation into active internal planning, even without a public timeline yet.

insights.claim: Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said during last month's investor call that a free offering could make sense in some markets but the company must be thoughtful about cannibalization of paid tiers, and that having an effective scaled ads business in any candidate country is 'clearly an important enabling factor' — concluding Netflix has 'no near-term plans to launch something.'
insights.speaker: Greg Peters (via Scharon Harding)
insights.so_what: Netflix explicitly naming cannibalization risk and a scaled-ads-business prerequisite means any free tier launch would likely be market-by-market and gated on ad infrastructure maturity — a more conservative and slower path than Disney's apparent posture.
insights.quote: A free offering could make sense in some markets, but we have to be thoughtful about cannibalization of paid tiers.

themes.theme: The price-hike backdrop driving this shift

insights.claim: Disney+ (131.6 million subscribers as of November) has raised US prices twice since 2024, most recently in October when ad plans rose $2/month and ad-free plans rose $3/month; Netflix (over 325 million subscribers as of January) also raised prices twice in the same period, most recently in March by $1/month (ad plans) or $2/month (ad-free plans).
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Concrete subscriber counts (131.6M and 325M+) and specific repeated price-hike amounts give a quantified baseline for modeling churn risk and the revenue tradeoff either company faces if it introduces a free tier that could cannibalize these large paid bases.

insights.claim: According to a Q3 2025 Parks Associates survey of 8,009 US households, 46 percent of US Internet households regularly use FAST (free ad-supported streaming television) services like The Roku Channel and Pluto TV to watch long-form video content.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding (citing Parks Associates)
insights.so_what: A 46% regular-usage rate for free ad-supported streaming among US households is a strong quantified indicator of mainstream consumer shift away from paid subscriptions, directly supporting the rationale for Disney and Netflix considering free tiers to capture this demand rather than cede it to Roku/Pluto.

insights.claim: A Q4 2025 survey of 4,493 people aged 18+ in the US and Canada found 54 percent of respondents use ad-supported subscription tiers, while AVOD/FAST adoption rose to 70 percent, up five percentage points year over year.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A 5-point YoY rise to 70% AVOD/FAST adoption is a clear accelerating-trend metric showing ad-supported and free streaming consumption is growing, not plateauing — a key demand-side data point for any streaming ad-revenue growth thesis.

insights.claim: The author frames the situation as ironic: years of price increases have driven customers toward free FAST alternatives, and now Disney and Netflix — companies whose earlier pivot from free broadcast/cable to paid subscription streaming helped create demand for cheaper alternatives — are themselves considering pivoting back toward free, ad-supported content.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: This framing captures a full-circle market dynamic in streaming economics: subscription fatigue driven by repeated price hikes is now forcing premium players back toward the ad-supported model they originally displaced, a cyclical pattern relevant for long-term streaming sector monetization strategy.
